lead: A bridge compares an unknown component against known ones and adjusts until a detector reads zero. At that null the balance equation gives the unknown directly, so the answer depends on ratios, not on source voltage or meter calibration. Wheatstone bridges do this for resistance, Kelvin bridges for very small resistance, and Maxwell, Hay and Schering bridges for inductance and capacitance at AC. Bridges sit inside sensor signal conditioning — strain-gauge load cells, RTDs, inductive and capacitive transducers — wherever a tiny impedance change must be read accurately.
prereq: You need Unit 2 (resistive transducers, strain gauges) and Unit 3 (inductive and capacitive transducers) for impedance ideas; see 6.1 for where a bridge output goes next.

sections.h3: Wheatstone bridge: four arms and a null

blocks.text: Four impedances form a diamond. A–B is Z1, A–C is Z2, B–D is Z3, C–D is Z4. The source drives A and D. A null detector connects B and C; it may be a galvanometer, a vibration galvanometer or a differential amplifier. Adjust one known arm until the detector reads zero. At that instant the potentials at B and C are equal.

blocks.where: Z1 to Z4 are the four arm impedances; at balance the detector between B and C carries no current. For pure resistances this becomes R1/R3 = R2/Rx, so Rx = R2R3/R1, where R1 is arm A–B, R2 is A–C, R3 is B–D and Rx is C–D.

items: Set the supply to a safe value and connect the detector between B and C.
Adjust the known arm for the smallest detector reading.
Check that the null is sharp, not a broad minimum.
Compute the unknown from the final arm values.

blocks.text: Near balance the detector output is proportional to the supply voltage and to the fractional change in the unknown. With one active arm, a 1% change in Rx gives about 0.25% of the supply voltage (V/400 for small changes), so a low-noise detector and the largest allowed supply improve sensitivity. Below about 1 Ω, lead and contact resistance add to the arms; the null then measures the leads as much as the unknown. Wheatstone bridges serve strain-gauge load cells, RTDs and resistor calibration.

sections.h3: Kelvin double bridge: four terminals for milliohms

blocks.text: A Kelvin double bridge is for resistances below about 1 Ω. It uses four terminals on the unknown: two current terminals carry the test current, and two potential terminals sense the voltage. The voltage drop in the current leads and contacts is outside the measured path. Two ratio pairs, outer R1–R2 and inner r1–r2, link through a low resistance r. Keep the potential leads separate from the current leads right up to the unknown.

blocks.where: Rx is the low unknown resistance, Rs is a known standard resistor, and R1 and R2 are the outer ratio arms. The equality holds when the inner ratio arms are set to the same ratio, r1/r2 = R1/R2; then the link and lead terms cancel.

blocks.text: The double bridge measures motor and transformer windings, busbar joints, switch contacts, shunts and cable resistance. Precision ohmmeters and LCR meters use the same four-terminal connection so probe leads do not enter the answer.

sections.h3: Maxwell, Hay and Schering: AC bridges

blocks.text: AC bridges balance complex impedances. The source is a sine wave, often 50 Hz, 1 kHz or 10 kHz. The detector is a tuned amplifier or a phase-sensitive detector. Balance needs equal magnitude and equal phase, so one control balances magnitude and another balances phase.

Maxwell bridge: the unknown Lx–Rx arm is balanced by R1 in parallel with C1. At balance Lx = R2R3C1 and Rx = R2R3/R1. Q = ωLx/Rx = ωR1C1. It suits Q from about 1 to 10. R2 and R3 are resistive arms, C1 is in farads, and ω = 2πf.

Hay bridge: the RC arm is series instead of parallel. At balance Lx = R2R3C1/(1 + ω²R1²C1²), with R1 in series with C1. In the Hay bridge Q = ωLx/Rx = 1/(ωR1C1), so ω²R1²C1² = 1/Q². For Q = 10 the correction term is 1/(1 + 1/Q²) = 0.99; for Q = 2 it is 0.80, which is why the bridge is used only above Q ≈ 10.

Schering bridge: the unknown Cx–Rx arm is balanced by standard capacitor C2, resistor R3 and a parallel R4–C4 arm. Balance gives Cx = C2R4/R3 and tan δ = ωR4C4. δ is the loss angle and tan δ the dissipation factor. High voltage stresses insulation, so the bridge tests cables, bushings and transformer insulation.

Match the bridge to the component before touching the controls. A Wheatstone bridge with resistive arms cannot balance an inductive arm: the inductive reactance has no resistive term to cancel it, so an AC bridge must include a reactance of the opposite sign. In an LCR meter the same bridges are switched automatically and the display shows L, C, R, Q or tan δ. Shield the bridge, keep detector leads short, balance magnitude first and then phase. Record the supply frequency because Maxwell and Hay formulas contain ω. The detector amplifier is a tuned stage; see 6.9.

examples.question: A Wheatstone bridge has R1 = 100 Ω in arm A–B, R2 = 200 Ω in arm A–C, R3 = 150 Ω in arm B–D and an unknown Rx in arm C–D. Find Rx at balance. A Maxwell bridge uses R2 = 1 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and C1 = 0.1 µF in parallel with R1. Find the inductance L.
steps: Wheatstone balance: R1/R3 = R2/Rx, so Rx = R2R3/R1.

traps: Using a Wheatstone bridge below about 1 Ω: lead and contact resistance then add to the arm and the null is wrong; use the Kelvin double bridge with four terminals.
Mixing bridge and quantity: Maxwell and Hay measure inductance, Schering measures capacitance and tan δ, Wheatstone and Kelvin measure resistance.
Forgetting the null: the bridge answer comes from the balanced arm values, not from the size of the detector reading at an arbitrary setting.
Unit slips in Maxwell and Hay: C1 must be in farads, so 0.1 µF is 0.1 × 10⁻⁶ F, and R values must be in ohms.
Using Maxwell for a high-Q coil or Hay for a low-Q coil: Maxwell suits Q from about 1 to 10, Hay suits Q above 10; Schering tan δ uses ω = 2πf.

quiz.q: State the balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge in terms of its four arms.
quiz.a: Z1/Z3 = Z2/Z4. For pure resistances, R1/R3 = R2/Rx.

quiz.q: Why does a Wheatstone bridge fail below about 1 Ω?
quiz.a: Lead and contact resistance become comparable with Rx, so the null shifts. The Kelvin double bridge separates current and potential leads to remove this error.

quiz.q: A Wheatstone bridge has R1 = 100 Ω, R3 = 150 Ω and R2 = 200 Ω. Find Rx at balance.
A Maxwell bridge has R2 = 1 kΩ, R3 = 10 kΩ and C1 = 0.1 µF. Find L.
Why is a Hay bridge preferred over a Maxwell bridge for Q > 10?
quiz.a: Hay uses a series RC arm. In the Hay bridge Q = ωLx/Rx = 1/(ωR1C1), so ω²R1²C1² = 1/Q². The balance term 1/(1 + ω²R1²C1²) is 0.99 at Q = 10 and 0.80 at Q = 2; it is close to 1 only at high Q, so Hay suits Q above about 10. Maxwell is used for Q from about 1 to 10.

quiz.q: In a Schering bridge, which element sets tan δ, and why is a high voltage used?
quiz.a: tan δ = ωR4C4, so the parallel capacitor C4 sets the dissipation factor. High voltage tests insulation at working stress and reveals cable, bushing and transformer faults.

quiz.q: Which bridge measures very low resistance, and what is special about its connections?
quiz.a: The Kelvin double bridge. It uses four terminals: two current terminals and two potential terminals, so lead and contact resistance cancel.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern sensor front ends replace manual nulling with auto-balancing digital bridges, and lock-in amplifiers recover tiny bridge outputs from noise. Impedance analysers sweep frequency and fit an equivalent circuit instead of balancing one arm. Search next for auto-balancing bridge, LCR meter, Kelvin connection, dissipation factor and impedance analyser.
